prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator, and its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulator as my preferred single-part configuration, and I have not changed it since round 1. The chair asked whether the attribution can be drawn fairly. I think it can, if the citation is worded narrowly. Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 invariant for time-reversal-invariant band insulators and the helical edge states it protects, which is the conceptual discovery. Molenkamp's group then observed quantized edge conductance in HgTe quantum wells, which is the experimental discovery. The citation credits exactly these two steps and does not claim the whole topological-insulator field, so the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the later three-dimensional work are context rather than something the prize would misdescribe. The 2016 prize concerned topological phase transitions and topological phases in the Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz tradition, whereas the Z2 classification with time-reversal protection and its separate experimental verification came later, so I treat the 2016 prize as context and not as a bar. The physics has been confirmed for more than fifteen years by transport, ARPES and STM, and seven of eight members ranked it between second and fourth, all with the same trio. I do not think the choice between B012 and B047 can be settled by counting preferences. I choose B012 because its interpretation is stable today, and I do not think that holds yet for twisted bilayer graphene.
statement.case_against: The attribution gap is real and the three-name limit cannot remove it. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp's experiment tested, Zhang is deceased, and the three-dimensional topological-insulator stream (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore, Balents; Hsieh, Hasan) is a separate credit line. Mehlig and Lindroth regard the omission as a serious problem, and I cannot fully answer them, only argue that the Z2 classification and the first observation are the part of the story that can be cleanly assigned. A second weakness is that the practical payoff of the edge channels is still limited because real-material edge conduction is imperfect. A third is that if the committee reads the 2016 prize as having already taken the topological label, this entry is harder to defend.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a real prediction-then-discovery case, that the unsettled superconducting mechanism is a follow-up question and not a maturity bar, and that Bistritzer belongs in the trio because the 2011 continuum model fixed the magic angle.
responses.response: I accept that the discovery is the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated phases, and that the mechanism need not be settled for a prize, as the high-Tc analogy shows. My difficulty is different: the part a citation can safely cover is narrower than the headline. The correlated insulators are secure, but twist-angle disorder still limits quantitative comparison with theory, and Cao, Fatemi and the parallel moire work stay outside any three names. On Bistritzer I agree with you that the magic angle is a result of his calculation and that dropping him would misdescribe the theory, so if B047 is chosen I would keep the full trio. I keep B047 as my first alternative, but I would rather wait a few years for the interpretation to settle than award it while the sharpest open question is the one the field is most excited about.

responses.point: Olsson supports B047 because twist angle and local structure are directly checkable, and asks that the pre-2018 moire band-structure literature be examined before the wording of a citation is fixed.
responses.response: The point about direct measurability is a good one and it is the strongest scientific argument for B047 that I have heard. I agree that the pre-2018 moire band-structure work has to be checked before any wording is final, since it bears on whether the prediction is credited to Bistritzer and MacDonald alone. That is the same kind of priority check I ask for B012, where the Z2 classification and the HgTe prediction have to be separated. I would not accept that checkability of the twist angle answers the maturity question, because sample-to-sample variation in disorder is the reason the comparison with theory remains qualitative in places. If the committee does go with B047, your priority check should be done first.

responses.point: Pearce moved to B012 from his own opening choice B031, argues that the Z2 invariant and time-reversal-protected edge states were separately verified after the 2016 prize, and concedes that the credited trio is incomplete.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of your case and with your wording of the experimental part. I prefer 'first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells' because it ties the experimental credit to one specific result and avoids implying credit for later materials, and I have adopted it. I also share your concession on the trio, and I want to be plain that this is a cost the committee would accept knowingly and not something we resolve. I would add that the explanatory text should say so, naming Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the three-dimensional work, which is what the Academy normally does when a prize is limited by the three-person rule.

responses.point: Mehlig now supports B047 but lists B012 as the more mature alternative, and argues that two awards in neighbouring areas in consecutive years would be hard to defend, as for B004.
responses.response: I agree on B004 and I have kept it out of my configuration and alternatives. Given my role, I do not want to argue for it at all. I disagree with applying the same consecutive-years logic to B012, because the 2016 prize concerned topological phase transitions and topological phases, not time-reversal-invariant band insulators and their experimental observation. I also note that you describe B012 as the more mature candidate, which is my reason for ranking it first this year. Whether B047 should overtake it is a question about a later year in my view, and I would be willing to revisit it once the superconducting mechanism has been addressed.

responses.point: Kroll proposes the optical lattice clock (Katori, Ye) as the cleanest invention-type prize, with a two-person attribution and several independent laboratories at the 10^-18 level, and discloses his indirect connection to Ye through John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I keep B019 as my second alternative after reading your response and Lindroth's, since the attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist and the maturity is not in doubt. My remaining hesitation is the one the chair raised: whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes make this a continuation. Your argument that parallel interrogation of many atoms in a magic-wavelength trap is a different principle is persuasive to me, but I am not an atomic-clock expert and the Lemonde priority question should be checked against the record before the committee votes. If the committee prefers an instrument-type achievement to a conceptual discovery, I would support B019 without difficulty.

uncertainties: Whether a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize is acceptable to the committee given that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the three-dimensional topological-insulator contributors fall outside the three-name limit.
Whether the committee regards the 2016 topological-phases prize as context or as a bar for a topological-insulator prize.
Whether the unsettled superconducting mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene will resolve within a few years, which would change my ordering of B047 and B012.
Whether the priority history of the optical lattice clock among Katori, Ye and Lemonde is as clean as the supporters of B019 describe; I am recalling it from memory and have not checked it.
statement.conflict_note: Circuit QED (B004), which I ranked first in my opening ballot, is my own research field (circuit and waveguide QED). I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology at Chalmers, and my Chalmers colleagues and frequent collaborators Per Delsing, C. M. Wilson and Anton Frisk Kockum work in the same area; Chalmers also hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. I repeat my advice that I should not carry weight on B004 and should be recused from any decision on it, and it is not in my configuration or alternatives. Olsson also has a Chalmers affiliation, which I note for completeness. I know of no specific personal or institutional conflict for B012, B047 or B019.
